canonical.name: Least absolute (centred) remainder modulo a positive integer m: existence, uniqueness under -m < 2r <= m, and the bound 4r^2 <= m^2
The centred residue quadruple of pm = a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2 has norm mn with 1 <= n < m
The residues of an integer square modulo 8 are 0, 1 and 4
No sum of three integer squares is congruent to 7 modulo 8
If 4 divides a sum of three integer squares then all three coordinates are even
Integers 4^a m with m = 7 mod 8 admit no four-square representation with a vanishing coordinate
Four-square representations of a prime need not be unique up to order and signs
Legendre's three-square theorem: every positive integer not of the form 4^a(8b+7) is a sum of three squares
canonical.reason: The converse of this page's obstruction. Every complete proof in the harvested sources needs either a genus or class-number argument for ternary forms or Minkowski's convex-body theorem, and in both cases Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions; the design for this page records it in the scope ledger rather than asserting it as an unproved remark, and plan-spec.json scaffolds no page for it.

sources.title: Keith Conrad, Proofs by Descent
sources.locator: §5 "Sum of two squares" and §6 "The four-square theorem", pp. 13-16, and Appendix C "Some results related to the four-square theorem", pp. 22-24, read in full. §§1-4 and §7 and Appendices A-B of the same document treat irrationality, Fermat's Last Theorem for n = 4, rational-function equations and Markov's equation, none of which is this page's subject.

contents.name: §5, Sum of two squares
Theorem 5.1, for a prime p with -1 a square mod p, p = x^2 + y^2, proved by descent on a multiple pd
Remark 5.2, Fermat's own descent from a counterexample, reported to Huygens
contents.reason: A historical note on how Fermat said he argued, without the argument; the library records mathematics it proves, and there is no proof here to record or to check.

contents.name: §6, The four-square theorem
Example 6.1, 2, 7, 15 and 23 have one four-square representation up to order while 65 has several
Lemma 6.2 (Euler, 1748), sums of four squares in Z are closed under multiplication, with the four displayed bilinear forms z1..z4
contents.note: Conrad's sign pattern is the one this page fixes, because it is the pattern Remark 6.7 shows the descent's divisibility step consumes.

contents.name: Remark 6.3, Euler's second choice of signs and Hamilton's quaternion choice
Lemma 6.4 (Euler, 1760), the congruence x^2 + y^2 + 1 = 0 mod p has a solution for every prime p
Remark 6.5, Euler's original homogeneous phrasing x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 0 mod p with a nonzero term, and the division that converts it
Theorem 6.6 (Lagrange, 1770), every n in Z+ is a sum of four integer squares
contents.note: Conrad states it for positive n; MIT Theorem 80 and Crisman Fact 14.2.2 state the nonnegative form this page adopts.

contents.name: Theorem 6.6 Step 1, there is k in Z+ with k < p and pk = x^2 + y^2 + 1
Theorem 6.6 Step 2, from pm a sum of four squares with 1 < m < p, a sum of four squares equal to pn with 1 <= n < m
Theorem 6.6 Step 3, the descent step is iterated until the multiplier reaches 1
Remark 6.7, the descent's divisibility step survives Euler's alternate signs but not Hamilton's quaternion signs
Appendix C, Some results related to the four-square theorem
contents.reason: The appendix holds Euler's rational four-square theorem and his generalised diagonal congruence; each is disposed on its own row below, and neither is load-bearing for the integral theorem this page proves.

contents.name: Theorem C.1 (Euler), every n in Z+ is a sum of four rational squares
Theorem C.2, for an odd prime p and a, b not divisible by p, the congruence ax^2 + by^2 = c mod p is solvable for every c
contents.reason: It generalises Lemma 6.4 to an arbitrary diagonal binary form and an arbitrary target class. Nothing on this page consumes more than the case a = b = 1 and c = -1, and which integers a binary quadratic form represents is the subject of the forms-and-reduction page at order 57.011.

sources.title: Joseph Lee and Abhinav Kumar, MIT 18.781 Theory of Numbers, Lecture 22: Four Squares Theorem
sources.locator: Lecture 22 in full, pp. 1-5: the note opens with the continuation of the Pell-Brahmagupta material from Lecture 21 and then proves the four-square theorem by quaternion norms and descent.

contents.name: Pell-Brahmagupta equation (continued): for solutions (x,y) and (z,w), x < z iff y < w iff x + sqrt(d) y < z + sqrt(d) w
contents.reason: The monotone ordering of Pell solutions by their real embedding is the tool that makes the fundamental solution well defined; it belongs with def-fundamental-pell-solution on the Pell page at order 57.015, and nothing about sums of squares uses it.

contents.name: Theorem 78, all positive solutions of x^2 - d y^2 = 1 are the coefficient pairs of powers of the least positive solution
contents.reason: This is the structure theorem for the Pell solution group, scaffolded as thm-all-positive-pell-solutions-are-fundamental-powers on the Pell page; it needs the ring Z[sqrt d] and its norm, neither of which this page introduces.

contents.name: Example (Putnam): infinitely many triples of consecutive integers each a sum of two squares
contents.reason: The construction turns the question into solving x^2 - 2y^2 = 1 and then quotes Pell solvability, so the example is a Pell application; the two-square arithmetic it uses is already developed at order 57.007.

contents.name: Proposition 79, if x^2 - d y^2 = N has one integral solution it has infinitely many
contents.reason: Scaffolded as cor-one-generalized-pell-solution-gives-infinitely-many on the Pell page; the proof multiplies by norm-one units of Z[sqrt d], machinery this page neither has nor needs.

contents.name: Example: n^2 + (n+1)^2 is a perfect square for infinitely many n
contents.reason: The example reduces to the negative Pell equation l^2 - 2m^2 = -1 and then quotes Proposition 79, so it is an application of Pell solvability rather than of any four-square result.

contents.name: Theorem 80 (Four Squares Theorem), every non-negative integer is a sum of 4 integer squares
contents.note: This source states the nonnegative form, which is the form this page adopts; Conrad Theorem 6.6 states the positive form.

contents.name: The real quaternions Q, the relations i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1, conjugation, and the norm ||z|| = a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2
contents.reason: The real quaternion algebra is not developed anywhere in this library at order 57.009: there is a quaternion group of order eight at order 68 but no division ring of quaternions and no norm map on one, and building that algebra would be a page of its own rather than a lemma of this one.

contents.name: Multiplicativity of the quaternion norm, giving the four-square product identity
contents.note: The identity is the same statement; this page proves it by expansion because the quaternion derivation would first require the algebra above. The sign pattern that falls out of the quaternion norm is Hamilton's, which Conrad Remark 6.7 shows the descent's divisibility step does not survive.

contents.name: Reduction of the theorem to n = 0, 1, 2 and to odd primes
Lemma 81, there is a positive integer m < p with mp a sum of four squares
Solvability of x^2 + y^2 + 1 = 0 mod p for odd p, by counting squares (stated inside Lemma 81)
The descent: halving the four coordinates when m is even, then reducing modulo an odd prime divisor l of m
contents.note: A different route past the same boundary: this source removes the even case by halving so it can use the strict bound |x'| < l/2 for odd l, while Conrad keeps |a'| <= m/2 for every m and excludes the equality case by hand. This page follows Conrad, so the equality case is a named step of lem-least-absolute-residue-quadruple-of-a-multiple.

sources.title: Evan Dummit, Number Theory (part 9): The Geometry of Numbers, 2022, v. 2.00
sources.locator: §9.1 "Minkowski's Convex-Body Theorem and Applications", subsections §9.1.1-§9.1.3, pp. 2-8, read in full. §§9.2-9.3 (ideal class groups, Minkowski's bound, binary quadratic forms) were not read for this pair.

contents.name: §9.1.1 Minkowski's Convex-Body Theorems
contents.reason: The whole subsection is lattice geometry in R^n: it needs full lattices, fundamental domains and Lebesgue measure, none of which is available at order 57.009, and the plan puts that development at order 111.047.

contents.name: Proposition (Blichfeldt's Principle), a bounded measurable set of measure greater than the covolume has two points differing by a lattice vector
contents.reason: Blichfeldt's principle is a measure-theoretic pigeonhole over a lattice quotient; it rests on the measure theory that the library reaches only in the 288-block, so it cannot be stated honestly on an elementary number-theory page.

contents.name: Theorem (Minkowski's Convex Body Theorem), a convex centrally symmetric open set of volume above 2^n times the covolume meets the lattice nontrivially
contents.reason: This is the geometric engine of every proof in §9.1.2, and it is precisely the tool the design for this page declines in favour of elementary descent; it is scaffolded for the Minkowski-theory page, where lattices and volumes exist.

contents.name: Theorem (Minkowski's Theorem for General Lattices)
contents.reason: The general-lattice form only restates the previous theorem after a linear change of coordinates, so it inherits the same unavailable prerequisites and belongs on the same later page rather than here.

contents.name: §9.1.2 Sums of Two and Four Squares
Theorem (Fermat's Two-Squares Theorem), every prime p = 1 mod 4 is a sum of two squares, by a lattice in R^2
Lemma 1 (Products of Sums of Four Squares), with the displayed four-square identity
contents.note: Dummit displays Euler's SECOND sign pattern (z2 = x1y2 - x2y1 + x3y4 - x4y3, z3 = x1y3 - x2y4 - x3y1 + x4y2, z4 = x1y4 + x2y3 - x3y2 - x4y1), which is Conrad's first alternate in Remark 6.3. Both patterns are identities and both support the descent; the item fixes Conrad's and rem-sign-patterns-in-the-four-square-identity records the disagreement.

contents.name: Remark: the four-squares identity as multiplicativity of the norm on the quaternion ring H, and H as a division ring
contents.reason: The ring of real quaternions and the fact that it is a division ring are not built anywhere in this library; the remark's content is the same algebra MIT Lecture 22 uses, and this page proves the identity by expansion instead.

contents.name: Lemma 2, for any prime p there are integers r, s with r^2 + s^2 = -1 mod p
Theorem (Lagrange's Four-Square Theorem), every positive integer is a sum of four squares, by a lattice in R^4
contents.note: The statement is included; the Minkowski route is not, for the reason recorded against the convex-body theorem above.

contents.name: Jacobi's formula: r4(n) = 8 sigma(n) for odd n and 24 sigma(d) for n = 2^k d with d odd
contents.reason: Counting representations is a statement about the divisor-sum function, and its proof needs theta series or the arithmetic of Hurwitz quaternions; the arithmetic-function page at order 348.001 is where sigma and its Dirichlet convolutions are built.

contents.name: §9.1.3 Sums of Three Squares
The obstruction: if n = 4^a (8b + 7) then n is not a sum of three squares, by reducing modulo 8 and inducting on a
contents.note: The source gives the statement and a two-sentence route ('for a = 0 this follows immediately by considering n modulo 8, and then one may induct on a') rather than a written proof, which is why the item's proof provenance is ai-altered and not literature-derived.

contents.name: Remark: the sums of three squares are not closed under multiplication, since 3 and 5 are sums of three squares and 15 is not
Theorem (Sums of 3 Squares, 3 Mod 8 Case), after Ankeny: every positive n = 3 mod 8 is a sum of three squares
contents.reason: The proof quotes Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions to choose an auxiliary prime and then applies Minkowski's convex-body theorem; the library has neither at order 57.009, and no page in plan-spec.json is scaffolded to build the three-square theorem.

contents.name: The modifications needed for the remaining residue classes of the three-square theorem
contents.reason: The source states these cases without proof and only indicates the changes to the lattice; recording an unproved converse of the obstruction is exactly what the design for this page declines, and no page is planned to carry Legendre's theorem in full.

sources.title: Karl-Dieter Crisman, Number Theory: In Context and Interactive
sources.locator: Ch. 14 "Beyond Sums of Squares", §14.2 "More Sums of Squares and Beyond", subsections §14.2.1-§14.2.2, printed pp. 241-243. §14.1 (the Gaussian-integer treatment of two squares) was not read for this pair.

contents.name: §14.2 More Sums of Squares and Beyond
§14.2.1 Summing more squares
Fact 14.2.1, Sums of three squares: n is a sum of three squares iff it is not an even power of two times an odd number congruent to seven modulo eight
contents.note: Only the obstruction half is built here. The source's phrasing 'an even power of two times an odd number congruent to 7 mod 8' is the same set as 4^a (8b+7); the item records that agreement. Crisman states the Fact without proof.

contents.name: Fact 14.2.2, Lagrange's four square theorem: any nonnegative integer may be written as a sum of four squares
contents.note: Independent corroboration of the nonnegative phrasing; the source explicitly skips the proof and points at the algebraic (quaternion) and geometric (Minkowski) routes.

contents.name: Example 14.2.3, the representation counts r_k(n), and Lagrange's theorem restated as r4(n) >= 1 for all n >= 0
contents.reason: r_k is an arithmetic function and the source forwards its computation to its own Theorem 25.8.1; the library builds arithmetic functions and their convolutions at order 348.001, and existence rather than counting is what this page proves.

contents.name: §14.2.2 Beyond squares
contents.reason: The subsection asks which integers are sums of cubes and of higher powers, which is Waring's problem; the number-theory track's scope denial 7 assigns Waring's problem and the circle method to a separate track and admits only Lagrange's four-square theorem here.

contents.name: Question 14.2.4, which numbers are sums of two, three, or k cubes, and Dickson's nine-cubes theorem
contents.reason: Sums of cubes have no elementary identity playing the role of Euler's, and Dickson's bound rests on extensive computation and the Hardy-Littlewood method; nothing in the library approaches either at this anchor.

contents.name: Question 14.2.5, sums of two cubes, two fourth powers, and two nth powers
contents.reason: Representation by two nth powers is Fermat-type Diophantine geometry, which the track's scope denial 5 assigns to elliptic curves and algebraic geometry rather than to this elementary block.
